title: Oneness, explained
hook: one common way to explain it: one Lord, alone worshiped, with names and attributes unlike any other

segments.voice: Yesterday, what it asks: the teeth on the testimony's key, and your line: knowing, sure, sincere. Did you check something you said against those three? Day one thousand sixty-nine.

"Say: He is Allah, the One!" A short surah, only a few lines in Pickthall's English. Sahih al-Bukhari records a man who heard another recite it over and over through the night. In the morning he told the Prophet about it, as if he thought it too little. His answer: by the One in whose hand my soul is, it equals a third of the Qur'an. A third, from a few short lines. Whatever those lines say about oneness must run deep. Today, the word Muslims use for that oneness, and one way teachers lay it out.

Tawhid. Making one, affirming oneness. It's the idea under la ilaha illallah. One common way to explain it splits it into three parts, so you can see oneness from three sides. First, one Lord. The opening surah says: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." One who creates, sustains and runs everything. Plenty of people, the Qur'an says, would agree with that much. If you ask who made the heavens and the earth, they will say Allah. Second, one alone worshiped. This is the side the shahadah presses hardest, the part this week has been circling. Acknowledging one Creator, and then still bowing to other things, isn't tawhid in this sense. Prayer, trust, deepest fear and hope, all go one way. Third, names and attributes unlike any other. Allah is called the Merciful, the Hearer, the Seer. People hear and see too, so how is that different? The Qur'an answers in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." The names are real, and nothing is like the one they name. The same surah closes: "And there is none comparable unto Him." That three-part way is not the only one. Other schools of Muslim theology explain oneness under different headings, and later this year has days for them. But the three sides make a simple frame to hold: one in who rules, one in who is worshiped, one in what He is like. One in every way.

The practice: reflect on one of the three. Settle, and breathe. Choose a side. One Lord: let your attention go to something you didn't make and can't keep running, your heartbeat, the weather, the light. One worshiped: ask quietly where your trust actually goes when things go wrong. Names unlike any other: take one word, merciful, and notice how far any mercy you've known falls short of the word. Stay with your one side, unhurried. If you pray, you can recite the surah of oneness. The bell holds the time.
Tawhid. Oneness: one Lord, one alone worshiped, and names nothing else can share. Today's word.
Your line: one in every way. Today, when you notice a sky, a meal, or a kindness, ask which of the three sides it touches. Tomorrow, the hidden partner. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims learn tawhid in early religious lessons, often through Surah al-Ikhlas (112), which can be recited in the daily prayers; some schools teach it in three parts, lordship, worship, and names and attributes, while others use different theological headings.

notes: Editor: hook corrected to Bukhari 5013's details (the listener, not the reciter, thought it too little); 'The Qur'an opens' changed to 'The opening surah says', since 1:2 in Pickthall's numbering follows the bismillah.
Pickthall 112:1, 112:4, 1:2 and 42:11 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording and punctuation.

Bukhari 5013 paraphrased (the man reciting it repeatedly, the oath 'by the One in whose hand my soul is', a third of the Qur'an); confirm number and details. The hook avoids the surah's number and ayah count in the voice ('a few lines').

The three-part division (rububiyyah, uluhiyyah, al-asma' wa al-sifat) is associated especially with Ibn Taymiyya and later Hanbali/Salafi teaching; Ash'ari and Maturidi theologians frame tawhid differently (e.g. oneness in essence, attributes and acts). The script calls it 'one common way' and names no school as right.
'Plenty of people, the Qur'an says, would agree' paraphrases 31:25 (also 29:61, 43:87).
howItsDone mentions surah 112 'which can be recited in the daily prayers'; a 'many' claim, Keeper may soften.
